formation.title: Three Crowns Under One Umbrella
formation.text:
For two hundred years after the fall of Pagan the Irrawaddy has been three kingdoms at war: Ava among the granaries of the dry zone, Hanthawaddy and its ports in the delta, and Prome on the river between them. Today the white umbrella stands over all three. Pegu, Prome and the upper capital answer to one throne, and the whole river from the Chindwin to the sea is ours.

The question every king of the united valley has had to answer is where to sit. Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung ruled from Pegu, where the ships of Bengal, Malacca and the Portuguese came to the brokers' halls and the Mon lords were won over rather than crushed. Their empire was the greatest the region had seen, and it fell apart within a generation of Bayinnaung's death. Thalun took the court back up the river to Ava in 1635, to the weirs, the rice and the service villages that filled the armies, and his realm lasted a century.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Rule from Hanthawaddy, among the ports and the Mon lords

modifiers.name: The Crown at Hanthawaddy
modifiers.text: The court sits at Pegu, the golden city of the Mon kings, where the royal brokers sell every foreign cargo and the war boats ride at the quays. The delta's lords serve the throne that honours them, and the far villages of the dry zone send fewer men to a capital they never see.

options.text: Rule from Ava, among the granaries and the service villages

modifiers.name: The Crown at Ava
modifiers.text: The court has gone back up the river to the heartland of the Burmese kings. Around the capital the ahmudan villages owe their men to the crown, the weirs of Kyaukse fill the royal granaries, and governors sent out from the palace hold the provinces close. The ports of the delta are left to them.

advances.name: The Weirs of Kyaukse
advances.text: The stone weirs and canals of the Panlaung and the Zawgyi, older than the Burmese themselves and extended by Anawrahta, water the Eleven Districts that were the granary of Pagan. Whoever holds them feeds the capital.

advances.name: The Wareru Dhammathat
advances.text: Wareru, the Mon king of Martaban, had the monks compile a law book from the older treatises of Pagan. It became the basic law of the delta and the model of every later Burmese code: inheritance, debt, marriage and the duties of each estate, written down.

advances.name: The Village Monastery
advances.text: Every village has its kyaung, and every boy spends some years in it as a novice, learning the Pali texts and the Burmese script from the monks. The kingdom reads more widely than its size or wealth would suggest.

advances.name: The Throne of Pagan
advances.text: Pagan fell to the Mongols in 1287, but its ten thousand temples still stand on the plain, and every king of the valley claims its throne. To rule the Irrawaddy is to be the heir of Anawrahta and Kyansittha.

advances.name: Martaban Jars
advances.text: The great glazed storage jars that went out through Martaban carried oil, rice, water and preserves on ships across the Indian Ocean, and the name of the port went with them from Gujarat to the Philippines.

advances.name: The City of Gems
advances.text: Thado Minbya built Ava at the meeting of the Myitnge and the Irrawaddy in 1365 and joined the broken courts of Pinya and Sagaing under it. The upper valley has one capital again.

event.title: The Founding of Ava
event.text:
In 1364 the Shan of Mong Mao sacked both Pinya and Sagaing, and the two rival courts of the upper valley were left in ruins. Thado Minbya, a prince of Sagaing, did not rebuild either. He drained the swamp where the Myitnge meets the Irrawaddy and in 1365 founded a new city there, Ava, the City of Gems, and joined the two kingdoms under it.

For the next four hundred years Ava would be what the outside world called Burma itself. Its kings claimed the throne of Pagan, its court wrote the language of the chronicles, and every later dynasty that united the valley came back to rule within sight of it.

options.text: A new city for an old throne.

advances.name: The Blood Drinkers
advances.text: The thwe thauk, the king's sworn companions, bind themselves to him and to one another by drinking a cup of their mingled blood. In battle they stand at the front, and they do not leave the field while he lives.

advances.name: The Fleets of Razadarit
advances.text: Razadarit of Hanthawaddy fought the Forty Years' War from the water: long war boats under many oars that came up the Irrawaddy to burn Ava's river towns and went down the coast to hold Martaban and Bassein.

advances.name: The Forty Years' War
advances.text: From 1385 to 1424 Ava and Hanthawaddy fought for the valley, a war of walled river towns besieged every dry season and lost again every rainy one. It taught the kingdom to hold its towns and to recover from its defeats.

event.title: The Forty Years' War
event.text:
In 1385 Razadarit of Hanthawaddy and the kings of Ava went to war for the valley, and for forty years neither could finish it. Ava's armies came down the river every dry season and besieged the Mon towns; Razadarit's war boats came up it and burned the river ports. Ava's crown prince Minyekyawswa, the greatest captain of the age, fell at Dala in 1417 and was mourned by his enemies. The war ended only when both its kings were dead, and left the Irrawaddy divided at Prome as it had begun.

The men who fought it learned that river towns are won by siege and that every gain upstream is lost the next rains. Some at court still say one more campaign will take the delta. Others say the river is a border worth keeping.

options.text: One more campaign will take the delta.

modifiers.name: The Delta Campaign
modifiers.text: The armies go down the river every dry season with siege engines and boats, and do not come home until the rains.

options.text: Let the river at Prome be the border.

modifiers.name: Peace on the River
modifiers.text: The war that bled both kingdoms is over. The fields are sown, the boats carry rice and not soldiers, and envoys go where armies went.

advances.name: The Gilding of the Shwedagon
advances.text: Queen Shin Sawbu terraced the hill of the Shwedagon, paved its summit and gave it her weight in gold; her heir Dhammazedi gave four times his. The great pagodas hold land, villages and servants of their own for their upkeep.

event.title: Shin Sawbu and the Monk
event.text:
Shin Sawbu was the daughter of Razadarit, a widow twice over, a hostage at the court of Ava for seven years, and from 1454 the queen of Hanthawaddy. She terraced the hill of the Shwedagon, paved its summit and gave it her own weight in gold for gilding. Her reign was remembered as the golden age of the Mon.

In old age she chose her heir not among the princes of her house but among the monks: Dhammazedi, the learned monk who had helped her escape from Ava. She made him leave the robes, married him to her daughter and gave him the throne. He ruled for twenty years, reformed the Sangha by the Kalyani ordination and gave the Shwedagon four times his weight in gold. Now the question is asked again: should the white umbrella pass by merit or by blood?

options.text: Give the throne to the wisest, as Shin Sawbu did.

modifiers.name: The Monk King
modifiers.text: A ruler raised in the monastery sits on the throne, and the Sangha and the learned are heard at court as never before.

options.text: The white umbrella belongs to the royal house.

modifiers.name: The White Umbrella
modifiers.text: The crown stays in the royal house, the princes and lords keep their place in the succession, and the court shines with the gold of an old dynasty.

advances.name: The Poets of Ava
advances.text: In the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries the monks and courtiers of Ava, Shin Maha Thilawuntha and Shin Maha Rahtathara among them, wrote the chronicles, the long pyo poems and the verse epistles that made Burmese a literary language.

advances.name: The Refuge at Toungoo
advances.text: When the Shan confederation sacked Ava in 1527, the people of the upper valley fled south to Toungoo, a small walled town in the hills that Mingyi Nyo had kept out of every war. The refugees made it the strongest state in the land.

advances.name: The Ports of Hanthawaddy
advances.text: Pegu, Bassein, Martaban and Syriam are the ports of the Bay of Bengal. Ships come from Gujarat, Bengal, Malacca and Aceh for rice, lac, jars and rubies, and every cargo passes through the hands of the king's sworn brokers.

advances.name: The Feringhi in Royal Pay
advances.text: Tabinshwehti hired Portuguese gunners and musketeers under Diogo Soares de Mello to take Martaban in 1541. From then on every Burmese king kept foreign soldiers of fortune in his pay.

advances.name: One Law, One Measure
advances.text: Bayinnaung ruled from Manipur to Lan Na and from the Shan hills to the sea. He gave the whole empire one law, one calendar and one set of weights and measures, so that a basket of rice and a tical of silver meant the same in every market.

advances.name: The Princes at Court
advances.text: The sons of vassal kings are raised at the Burmese court as pages and companions of the princes. Naresuan of Ayutthaya was one of them. They learn the ways of their overlord, and their fathers keep faith while they are there.

advances.name: The Bayingyi
advances.text: The Portuguese of Syriam, taken in 1613 and settled as a hereditary service community, serve the crown as its gunners and musketeers. Their descendants keep their faith and their names for centuries.

event.title: The Fall of Syriam
event.text:
For thirteen years the Portuguese adventurer Felipe de Brito held the port of Syriam as his own kingdom, plundered the pagodas of the delta for their bells and taxed every ship that came up the river. In 1613 King Anaukpetlun took Syriam after a siege of months, and de Brito was impaled before its walls.

Some four or five thousand Portuguese, their families and their mixed sons are now our captives. They are good gunners and better musketeers, and they know the ways of the foreign merchants. The court must decide what to do with them.

options.text: Settle them in the Mu valley as the crown's gunners.

modifiers.name: The Bayingyi Villages
modifiers.text: Between the Mu and the Chindwin the Portuguese captives till land given by the crown, keep their priests and their faith, and owe the king their sons as gunners and musketeers.

options.text: Keep the Feringhi at court as interpreters and traders.

modifiers.name: The Feringhi Quarter
modifiers.text: The Portuguese of Syriam live by the capital, interpret for the court, broker for the foreign merchants and pray in their own church.

advances.name: The Ahmudan
advances.text: The ahmudan are the crown's service people: whole villages around the capital, each bound to a regiment, a guard, the boats or the elephants, owing a set number of men in exchange for land. Thalun widened the system and brought it under the palace.

advances.name: The Sittan
advances.text: Thalun's revenue inquest of 1635 recorded every village, its land, its families and their dues. It gave the crown the first count of its people and the means to take what it was owed.

event.title: The Revenue Inquest of 1635
event.text:
King Thalun has done what no king of the valley did before him. His officers went to every village of the kingdom and wrote down its land, its people, the service group each family belonged to and what it owed the crown in men, rice and silver. The registers of the sittan, as the inquest is called, are bound and kept at the palace.

From them the court has its first count of the kingdom: about two million souls. For the first time the king knows what his realm can give him, and the lords who stood between him and the villages can no longer hide what they hold.

options.text: Every village is on the king's register.

advances.name: The Teak Yards
advances.text: Burmese teak is the finest ship timber in the East. English country traders build and repair their ships at Syriam, and from 1729 the French Company keeps a yard there for Pondicherry.

advances.name: The Royal War Boats
advances.text: The crown's war boat regiments, drawn from ahmudan villages along the river, man long gilded boats of sixty oars with a gun in the bow and musketeers amidships. On the Irrawaddy nothing can stand against them.

advances.name: The Great Chronicle
advances.text: U Kala's Maha Yazawin, finished about 1724, gathered the histories of Pagan, Ava, Hanthawaddy, Arakan and the Shan into one chronicle of the Burmese kingdom. Every later history of the realm was written from it.

advances.name: The Gun Companies
advances.text: The Restored Toungoo kings at Ava turn more of the service villages over to the gun. Their companies owe musketeers by birth, as other villages owe boatmen or elephant men, and draw their weapons from the royal arsenal.

advances.name: The Hluttaw
advances.text: The Hluttaw, the council of the four wungyi ministers, sits in the palace to hear the business of the realm, try great cases and send out the royal orders. Nothing leaves the palace without its seal.

advances.name: The Rising at Moksobo
advances.text: In 1752 the hunter Aung Zeya refused to swear to the Mon conquerors of Ava, raised the forty six villages of the Mu valley and founded the Konbaung dynasty as Alaungpaya. His musketeers took back the whole valley in eight years.

event.title: The Hunter of Moksobo
event.text:
In 1752 the restored kingdom of Hanthawaddy took Ava and carried the last Toungoo king south as a captive. In the village of Moksobo, among the dry hills of the Mu valley, the headman Aung Zeya, a hunter, refused to drink the water of allegiance to the Mon. He called out the forty six villages of his district, fortified Moksobo with a stockade, and beat back every force sent against him.

He has taken the name Alaungpaya, the future Buddha, and the whole north has come to his drum. Ava is retaken and the army stands at the edge of the delta. In the capture of the pagoda town of Dagon he sees the end of the war and means to found a city there called Yangon, the End of Strife.

options.text: Every village answers the hunter's drum.

modifiers.name: The Hunter's Call
modifiers.text: The villages of the north muster behind the man who would not swear to the Mon, and every headman brings his men.

options.text: Found Yangon: let there be an end of strife.

modifiers.name: The End of Strife
modifiers.text: A new city rises beside the Shwedagon, and the conquered delta is bound to the crown by a port that faces the sea.

advances.name: The Cassay Horse
advances.text: The Manipuri horsemen carried off in the campaigns of 1758 and 1764 and their sons form the cavalry of the Konbaung army. The Burmese call them Kathe; the British will call them the Cassay Horse.

advances.name: The Stockades of Bandula
advances.text: Burmese armies can throw up a stockade of heavy timber and earth along a river within weeks and hold it against any assault. Maha Bandula's stockade at Danubyu ran for a mile along the water.

advances.name: The Marionette Stage
advances.text: Under Singu the court minister of royal entertainment, U Thaw, gave the yoke thé its fixed troupe of characters, kings, ministers, hermits and spirits. At a pwe the puppets may mock what no courtier dares to name.

advances.name: The Earth Oil of Yenangyaung
advances.text: Along the middle Irrawaddy hereditary twinza families draw earth oil from hand-dug wells and send it down the river in jars, to light the lamps of the kingdom and to preserve its teak. Hiram Cox counted 520 wells on the royal register.

advances.name: The Four Invasions
advances.text: Between 1765 and 1769 the Qing sent four armies against Burma, and all four were broken in the hills and the fevers of the frontier. An invader who comes in force will find the land itself his enemy.

event.title: The Truce of Kaungton
event.text:
Four times in four years the Qing emperor sent his armies down from Yunnan, and four times the hills, the rains and the fevers of the frontier broke them before the Burmese armies did. At Maymyo in 1768 the banner army of Ming Rui was destroyed and its general took his own life. In December 1769 the last invasion lay starving and sick at Kaungton, and the Burmese commander Maha Thiha Thura, rather than destroy it, let it march home under a truce agreed between the generals.

King Hsinbyushin was not asked. He is furious that the enemy who came four times was allowed to leave alive, and he has torn up his copy of the truce. The generals wait in the Shan hills, not daring to come before him.

options.text: Honour the generals' truce and let the dragon sleep.

modifiers.name: The Truce Honoured
modifiers.text: The court keeps the word its generals gave. The northern border is quiet, the army comes home and the envoys of Yunnan are received.

options.text: Send Maha Thiha Thura a woman's dress.

modifiers.name: The King's Wrath
modifiers.text: The king who was not consulted has shamed his victorious generals before the court. No commander will make terms again without the palace, and the great lords remember it.

destiny.name: Lord of the White Umbrella
destiny.text: Ava, Pegu and Prome answer to one throne, and the white umbrella stands over the whole river. Every king who united the valley found that holding it together was harder than winning it. Keep the realm at stability 25 to open the road chosen at the formation: the sea from Hanthawaddy, or the frontiers from Ava.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: Lord of the White Umbrella
event.text:
The realm has held together. The lords of Pegu and Martaban, the governors of Prome and the service villages of the dry zone send their tribute to one palace, and the chroniclers have begun to write of the three crowns as one kingdom.

The kings of the united valley never stood still for long. Those who ruled from Pegu looked to the sea and its ports; those who ruled from Ava looked to the hills and the frontiers beyond them. The road this crown chose at its founding now lies open.

options.text: The umbrella stands over the whole river.

destiny.name: The Tenasserim Coast
destiny.text: South of Martaban the coast runs down to Tavoy, Tenasserim and the island harbour of Mergui, where the ships of Bengal and the Coromandel landed cargoes for the overland road to Siam. The Mon kings, Ayutthaya and Bayinnaung all fought for it. A crown that lives by the sea must hold the ports of the whole coast, down to the crossing of the Pakchan at Kraburi. Required: own Mergui and Kraburi, and 1,000 gold in the treasury.

conditions.text: Chose to rule from Hanthawaddy
Own Mergui, or a subject owns it
Own Kraburi, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: The Ports of the South
event.text:
Mergui and Kraburi are ours. The harbour masters who answered to Ayutthaya now answer to Pegu, and the ships that come in on the monsoon from Bengal and the Coromandel coast pay their dues to our officers.

From Martaban to the Pakchan the whole coast is in one hand for the first time since Bayinnaung. The merchants of the delta say the next prize lies further south, where the tin of Junk Ceylon is loaded.

options.text: Every port of the coast pays its dues to Pegu.

destiny.name: The Golden City
destiny.text: The Venetian Cesare Fedrici and the Englishman Ralph Fitch saw Pegu in the 1560s and 1580s and could not find words for it: the gilded palace, the moat full of crocodiles, the streets wide enough for elephants, the king's brokers selling every foreign cargo at fixed fees. Grow Pegu by half, from its 27 of 1337 to 41, keep brokers' halls in two delta towns, and take Thalang, the tin island of Junk Ceylon whose metal came to the Mergui ships. Required: also 2,000 gold.

conditions.text: Own Thalang, or a subject owns it
Pegu is ours and has grown to at least 41 development (from 27 in 1337)
We have a Brokers' Hall in at least two of our towns
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Golden City
event.text:
Foreign travellers no longer believe what they are told about Pegu until they see it. The city has grown past its old walls, the brokers' halls are full, and tin from Junk Ceylon lies on the quays beside the rice and the lac.

The court is divided over what the city should become. Some would follow Bayinnaung and build a palace and walls that tell every envoy whose city this is. Others would follow his brokers, and put every foreign cargo through the king's hands.

options.text: Raise a new palace and walls, as Bayinnaung did.

modifiers.name: The Palace of Kanbawzathadi
modifiers.text: A new palace rises at Pegu with walls, a moat and a gate for every vassal kingdom that built it. Envoys are dazzled, and the villages that sent men to dig the moat sowed less rice.

options.text: Every cargo passes through the king's brokers.

modifiers.name: The King's Brokers
modifiers.text: Every foreign cargo at Pegu is sold through the king's brokers at fixed fees, and the lords who once took their share of the trade are left with nothing.

destiny.name: Emporium of the Bay
destiny.text: In 1337 the market of the Mon country sat at Martaban. Bayinnaung's Pegu drew the trade of the whole bay to itself: rubies, musk, lac and rice going out, the cloth of the Coromandel and the porcelain of China coming in. Make Pegu the seat of its own market and double it from its 1337 value, to 54. Required: also 3,000 gold and 75 prestige.

conditions.text: Pegu is ours and is the seat of a market
Pegu is ours and has grown to at least 54 development (from 27 in 1337)
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Emporium of the Bay
event.text:
Pegu is the market of the whole coast now. Martaban, Syriam and Bassein send their goods up to it, and merchants from Bengal, the Coromandel, Aceh and Malacca keep factors in its streets. The king's customs fill a treasury that the kings of Ava could never have imagined.

What Pegu does with this wealth will decide what kind of power it is. It can put war boats and teak hulls on every route of the bay, or it can open its gates to every nation that trades there.

options.text: Put our ships on every route of the bay.

modifiers.name: Ships for Every Shore
modifiers.text: Teak hulls built in the delta yards and the king's war boats sail every route of the bay, from Chittagong to Aceh.

options.text: Let every nation keep its quarter in Pegu.

modifiers.name: A City of All Nations
modifiers.text: Armenians, Muslims of the Coromandel, Portuguese and Chinese each keep their quarter, their headman and their temple in Pegu. Envoys and learned men come with the merchants, and the monks do not like the foreign temples.

destiny.name: The Sawbwas Bow
destiny.text: The Shan princes of the hills east of the dry zone sacked Pinya and Sagaing in 1364 and ruled Ava itself for half a century after 1527. Bayinnaung broke them in 1557, and every king of Ava after him kept their sons at court and their tribute in his treasury. Take Hsipaw and Mong Nai, and build the weirs of the dry zone in three places to feed the armies that go up into the hills.

conditions.text: Chose to rule from Ava
Own Hsipaw, or a subject owns it
Own Möngnai, or a subject owns it
We have a Kyaukse Weir in at least three of our locations

event.title: The Sawbwas Bow
event.text:
The sawbwas of Hsipaw and Mong Nai have come down from the hills to kneel in the palace and drink the water of allegiance. Their sons will stay at court, their tribute will come every year, and their men will march with ours.

It took the weirs of the dry zone to do it: an army that goes into the Shan hills must carry its rice with it, and only the granaries of Kyaukse could fill the carts.

options.text: The hills send their tribute to Ava.

destiny.name: The Mahamuni Comes to Ava
destiny.text: In 1784 the crown prince crossed the Arakan Yoma and took Mrauk U, and the next year the Mahamuni, the image the Arakanese believed was cast in the Buddha's lifetime, was carried over the mountains to the capital. Manipur had fallen to Alaungpaya in 1758 and would fall again in 1814. Take Mrauk U and Imphal, grow Ava by half from its 1337 value, to 47 (the map has no Ava; Pinya, a few miles from it, stands for it), and hold 50 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Mrauk U, or a subject owns it
Own Imphal, or a subject owns it
Pinya, standing for Ava, is ours and has grown to at least 47 development (from 31.5 in 1337)
Prestige at least 50

event.title: The Mahamuni Comes to Ava
event.text:
Mrauk U has fallen and Manipur is ours. Over the passes of the Arakan Yoma a column of thousands drags the Mahamuni image towards the capital on rafts and sledges, and the villages along the road come out to gild it as it passes. Behind it march the captives of Arakan and Manipur: craftsmen, boatmen, astrologers and the Manipuri horsemen the court calls Cassay.

The king must decide what this conquest is to mean.

options.text: Enshrine the image and open its gates to pilgrims.

modifiers.name: The Mahamuni Enshrined
modifiers.text: Pilgrims from every province come to the capital to press gold leaf on the Mahamuni, and the faith of the kingdom gathers around the image its king keeps.

options.text: Settle the captives in their own quarters by the capital.

modifiers.name: The Captive Quarters
modifiers.text: Arakanese and Manipuri captives live in their own quarters around the capital as the crown's craftsmen, boatmen and horsemen. Their work is good, and they remember where they came from.

destiny.name: The Brahmaputra
destiny.text: In 1817 a Burmese army crossed the Patkai into Assam, and by 1822 the Ahom throne was held by a king of Ava's choosing and Burmese garrisons stood at Gauhati on the Brahmaputra. It was the furthest the kingdom ever reached, and it brought the war with the East India Company in 1824. Take Charaideo, the old seat of the Ahom kings, and Guwahati, double Ava from its 1337 value, to 63, and hold 75 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Charaideo, or a subject owns it
Own Guwahati, or a subject owns it
Pinya, standing for Ava, is ours and has grown to at least 63 development (from 31.5 in 1337)
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Brahmaputra
event.text:
Our garrisons stand at Gauhati, and the Ahom throne is held by a king who owes it to Ava. No Burmese army has ever stood so far from the Irrawaddy. Beyond the river lies Bengal, and in Bengal the East India Company.

Maha Bandula, the general who took Assam, wants to go on. With Arakan and Assam in our hands, he says, Bengal can be taken from both sides at once. Others at court say that the Company is not the Ahom king, and that what is held should be held well.

options.text: Let Bandula march on into Bengal.

modifiers.name: Bandula's March
modifiers.text: The armies of Arakan and Assam make ready to strike into Bengal from two sides. The stockades fall and the plunder comes home, and every neighbour watches the kingdom with fear.

options.text: Hold the valley through an Ahom king of our choosing.

modifiers.name: The King at Jorhat
modifiers.text: An Ahom king of Ava's choosing sits at Jorhat, Burmese stockades hold the passes and the river crossings, and the valley is kept without another war.

units.name: Thwe Thauk
units.text: The king's sworn companions, bound by a cup of mingled blood. A small company of heavy infantry that strikes hard and does not break.

units.name: Hanthawaddy War Boat
units.text: A long Mon war boat under many oars, quick on the river and along the coast, carrying archers and a swivel piece. Its light hull breaks sooner than a sea galley's.

units.name: Bayingyi Gunners
units.text: Descendants of the Portuguese of Syriam, hereditary gunners of the Burmese crown. Quicker to fire and heavier in the barrage than the royal train, and harder to keep supplied with powder and shot.

units.name: Irrawaddy War Boat
units.text: A gilded royal war boat of sixty oars with a gun in the bow and musketeers amidships. Fast and well armed, thin in the hull.

units.name: Cassay Horse
units.text: Manipuri horsemen of the Konbaung army, quick to strike and hard on a wavering enemy, but never a large corps.

units.name: Toungoo Militia
units.text: The townsmen and refugees of Toungoo, raised with spear, shield and the first matchlocks.

units.name: Ahmudan Service Regiment
units.text: Men of the crown's service villages, owed to the king by birth and called out by regiment.

units.name: Thenat Musketeers
units.text: Ahmudan companies that owe the king guns rather than spears, drilled by regiment and armed from the palace arsenal.

units.name: Konbaung Musketeers
units.text: The musketeers of the northern villages who followed Alaungpaya out of Moksobo.

buildings.name: Kyaukse Weir
buildings.text: A stone weir and its feeder canals on a river of the dry zone, watering the rice fields beside it and rebuilt every dry season by the corvee of the villages it waters.

where.text: The location's raw material is Rice

buildings.name: Kyaung
buildings.text: A teak village monastery where the monks teach the boys of the village to read and write.

buildings.name: Martaban Kilns
buildings.text: Long wood-fired kilns of the Mon country where the great glazed jars of Martaban are thrown and fired.

buildings.name: Brokers' Hall
buildings.text: The hall of the king's sworn brokers, through whose hands every foreign cargo of the port must pass.

buildings.name: Pagoda Trust
buildings.text: The lands, villages and hereditary servants given to a great pagoda for its gilding, its lamps and its festivals.

where.text: Is location holy site for is Theravāda

buildings.name: Teak Shipyard
buildings.text: A delta yard where Burmese teak is sawn and fitted into ships for the crown and for foreign merchants.

buildings.name: Hluttaw
buildings.text: The council hall in the palace where the four wungyi sit to hear the business of the realm and seal the royal orders.

buildings.name: River Stockade
buildings.text: A stockade of heavy teak trunks and earth along the river bank, with guns on the water face.

buildings.name: Yoke Thé Stage
buildings.text: A marionette stage where the puppeteers of the town play the Jataka tales and the follies of the court.

buildings.name: Twinza Wells
buildings.text: Hand-dug earth-oil wells held by the hereditary twinza families, worked with rope, bucket and windlass.

buildings.name: Mahamuni Shrine
buildings.text: The pagoda in the capital where the Mahamuni image sits, carried from Mrauk U in 1785. Pilgrims from the whole kingdom come to press gold leaf on it, and the king who keeps it is the keeper of the most sacred image of the land.

list.name: The Myowun
list.text: From 1649 the kings at Ava no longer sent their brothers and sons to rule Prome and Toungoo as viceroys. They sent myowun instead: governors of no royal blood, appointed and recalled at the king's pleasure. By the 1680s the grown princes were kept at Ava as myoza, living on the revenue of towns they never governed, and the provincial seats from which princes had so often rebelled were held by men with no claim to the throne.

conditions.text: Has advance The Sittan

list.name: The Nakhandaw
list.text: The nakhandaw, the royal reporters, carry each order written at the Byedaik to the Hluttaw and sit through its sessions to tell the king what was said there. Others are posted in the towns of the kingdom to report on its governors and headmen. John Crawfurd, envoy to Ava in 1827, called them authorised spies.

list.name: The Thathanabaing
list.text: The king names the Thathanabaing, primate of the sangha, from among the most learned monks, usually a villager's son with no tie to the royal house. Bodawpaya set the Sudhamma Council of elder monks beside him in 1784 and ended the quarrel over wearing the robe on one shoulder or both that had divided the order for most of a century. Under the primate the gaing-gyok judge the monks of each district, the Mahadan Wun disciplines them, and the Wutmye Wun keeps the register of religious lands, so that true endowments stay free of tax and false ones do not.

conditions.text: Theravāda religion

list.name: The Akaukwun
list.text: The Akaukwun collects the king's customs from every ship that enters the delta port: Syriam until Alaungpaya sacked it in 1756, Rangoon after. The office is often given to a foreign merchant who knows the trade of the Bay of Bengal. In 1760 it was held by Gregory the Armenian, whom the English called the Shahbandar of Rangoon.

list.name: The Myothugyi
list.text: Every township has its myothugyi, a headman from a family that has held the office for generations. He keeps the rolls of households and land, settles disputes, sends the revenue to the nearest treasury and the men the levy calls for. The office passes to his son, and only when a line dies out does the Hluttaw name a new one. The prince or minister who holds a town as its myoza reaches its revenue only through him.
